analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law limiting a president's power to withhold money Congress has appropriated.
analysis.headline: The bill, a single sentence introduced in the closing weeks of the 118th Congress, drew zero cosponsors and died in the Senate Budget Committee with no hearing and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill repeals the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, the law that stops a president from simply refusing to spend money Congress has appropriated. Today a president can propose canceling a spending item, but Congress must approve the cut. Repeal would leave no process at all, handing the White House sole discretion over whether the people's money gets spent.
analysis.who_benefits: The sitting president and future presidents, who would gain the power to withhold or permanently cancel spending Congress approved without ever asking lawmakers. A White House could defund programs it dislikes simply by not spending the money, and agencies would gain leverage over Congress rather than the reverse.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the only law that requires a president to report and win Congress's approval before permanently canceling (rescinding) appropriated funds, leaving the White House with unilateral control over whether appropriated money is ever spent.

Eliminates the expedited procedures Congress uses to consider a president's proposed spending cuts, so no structured process — congressional or otherwise — would govern presidential withholding of funds.

analysis.who_pays: Federal programs and the people who rely on them: money Congress appropriated could go unspent at the White House's discretion. States, grantees, and contractors would lose the legal assurance that approved funds will actually arrive, and Congress loses its hold on the purse.

drawbacks.text: A president could decline to spend money Congress specifically directed to programs — the exact practice Congress passed the 1974 law to stop, when a previous administration withheld funds for projects it opposed.

Repeal would create legal chaos rather than clean flexibility: the Constitution gives Congress the power of the purse, so a president refusing to spend appropriated money would invite immediate court fights, leaving states and grantees unable to plan.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill is that presidents need faster ways to cut wasteful spending; an honest supporter must acknowledge that this bill replaces a slow congressional approval process with no process at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The flexibility a president would gain is narrow: under current law a president can already propose rescissions and Congress can approve them quickly. The cost is far larger — eliminating Congress's only structured check on a president refusing to spend money the people's representatives appropriated. As drafted, a single sentence of repeal with no replacement mechanism, the bill is a pure transfer of spending power from Congress to the White House.

outcome.mechanism: One senator introduced it in the last three weeks of the session, and the Senate Budget Committee never took it up before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the one-sentence repeal on December 16, 2024, in the closing weeks of the 118th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Budget Committee, where no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
Not a single senator joined as a cosponsor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without any floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Congress keeps the Impoundment Control Act, so a president still cannot permanently cancel money Congress appropriated without lawmakers' approval; the presidency gains nothing.

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the one-sentence repeal on December 16, 2024; no other member joined him.

for.name: Russell Vought
for.role: President-elect Trump's nominee for budget director
for.what_they_did: Had publicly argued the Impoundment Control Act is unconstitutional and that a president may refuse to spend appropriated funds, keeping the issue alive heading into the new administration.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on referral on December 16, 2024, and scheduled no hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no debate or vote, so no partisan split appears anywhere in the record.

industries.note: Repeal would give the White House sole discretion to withhold or permanently cancel money Congress appropriated, removing the requirement that Congress approve any rescission. That is a direct transfer of spending power from lawmakers to one officeholder.

industries.industry: Federal grantees, contractors, and state governments
industries.note: These interests depend on appropriated funds actually being spent. Repeal would strip away the legal backstop guaranteeing it, since a president could withhold money with no congressional review.
